At the Thursday science club, Aadhya, ten, raised her hand before Naveen Sir had even finished the attendance.

"Sir, why does the moon look huge when it's rising and small when it's high up?"

Naveen Sir smiled. "It's not in our syllabus. What do you think?"

"Maybe it's closer when it rises?"

"How could you check?"

That week, Aadhya held a one-rupee coin at arm's length every evening and covered the moon with it, once low over the buildings and once high in the sky. The coin covered it both times.

"It's the same size!" she told the club the next Thursday. "So why does it look bigger?"

Naveen Sir handed her a library book on illusions. She read it on the bus home.

qa.q: What did Aadhya use to cover the moon?
qa.a: She held a one-rupee coin at arm's length.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when the coin covered the moon both times?
qa.a: Aadhya felt surprised and excited, and even more curious about why it looked bigger.

qa.q: How did Naveen Sir support Aadhya's curiosity?
qa.a: He asked what she thought and how she could check, then gave her a book, so she investigated herself.

qa.q: How might the other club members react to Aadhya's findings?
qa.a: They might be surprised and curious too, wanting to try the coin test themselves.

grounding: At a school science club, a child asks a question beyond the syllabus and investigates it on her own.

I'm Lokesh, Afreen's big brother. During the monsoon, our garden in Pune fills with snails, and this year my sister, nine, got obsessed.

Every morning she went out with an old notebook and a torch. She wrote down how many snails were on the wall, the steps and the tulsi pot. She asked me why they came out after rain and hid in the sun. I didn't know.

She borrowed my phone to look it up, then found a library book about molluscs. Nobody asked her to. It wasn't homework.

By August, her notebook had drawings of shells, dates, and arrows. I'm not sure what she felt, but she was up before anyone else every day.

qa.q: Where did Afreen count the snails?
qa.a: She counted the snails on the wall, the steps and the tulsi pot.

qa.q: What might Afreen have been feeling during the monsoon mornings?
qa.a: Lokesh couldn't be sure, but she seemed curious and eager, getting up before anyone else.

qa.q: How could the family encourage Afreen's inquiry?
qa.a: Give her time and books, ask about her notebook, and help her find answers to her questions.

qa.q: How does Lokesh see his sister's snail project?
qa.a: Lokesh is impressed and a little puzzled, noticing she did it without being asked.

grounding: An older brother observes his sister investigating snails in the monsoon out of curiosity, beyond homework.

The summer I was ten, the lane split into two gangs. There was the cricket gang, which I joined, and the cycle gang, which Gargi led.

We had rules. Cricket gang members wore caps backwards and met at the empty plot at five. Cycle gang members rode in a line and wouldn't let anyone walk with them.

For weeks, we didn't talk to them. It felt important, like being on a team.

Then Gargi's chain broke, and nobody in her gang knew how to fix it. I did. I fixed it, and she let me ride at the back.

Looking back, the gangs made us feel we belonged. But they also made us miss out on each other. I'm Kiran, and I still have that cap.

qa.q: What did cricket gang members do with their caps?
qa.a: They wore caps backwards.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel about being in the cricket gang?
qa.a: Kiran felt proud and included, as if being on a team was important.

qa.q: What could the children have done to belong without shutting others out?
qa.a: They could keep their groups but also play together sometimes, as when Kiran fixed Gargi's chain.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Kiran after the chain was fixed?
qa.a: Gargi was likely grateful and began to see Kiran as a friend, not a rival.

grounding: A child looks back on a summer when friend groups formed with shared interests and boundaries.

Durga Puja holidays, Saturday

Big fight with Ishita today. We were practising the dance for the building function, and she said I was always in the front. I said she never learns the steps.

Ganga

Devika, come here. You were interrupting your friend again on the phone. Let your Preeti Dadi tell you something.

When I was ten, my best friend Kamla came to my house and said her father's shop had burned down. I was so eager to help that I kept talking: "Don't worry, my father will help, we'll give you money..." She stopped talking.

My mother took me aside. "Look at her shoulders," she said. Kamla's were hunched, her eyes on the floor.

So I went back and just sat. I didn't say anything. After a while, Kamla told me everything, how scared she was.

That's when I learned, Devika: listening is not waiting to talk. It's watching too.

qa.q: What happened to Kamla's father's shop?
qa.a: Her father's shop had burned down.

qa.a: Kamla felt overwhelmed and scared, which is why she stopped talking and hunched her shoulders.

qa.a: Preeti's mother pointed out Kamla's body language, so Preeti sat quietly, which let Kamla share her fears.

qa.q: How might Preeti's mother have felt watching her daughter?
qa.a: Her mother was likely concerned and wanted to teach her kindly how to listen.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at ten, she learned to listen without interrupting and to read a friend's body language.

"My dog is at the vet."

Pankaj almost said, "Mine got sick once too!" but stopped. He saw that Ojas's hands were twisting his tie and his eyes were red.

Ojas kept talking. "Mummy says he might need an operation."

In the colony library in Kolkata, Jahnavi, eight, was stuck on her maths homework.

"Twelve plus seven is nineteen," she said to her brother Yash. "But what's nineteen minus seven?"

Yash, eleven, smiled. "Think. You added seven to get nineteen. What if you take it away again?"

Jahnavi frowned. Then her face lit up. "Twelve! Because it goes back!"

"Exactly."

She tried another. "Five plus eight is thirteen. So thirteen minus eight is five!"

She wrote three more pairs, grinning. "It's like walking forward and then walking back."

When I was eleven, I had a huge pile of animal cards. Chinmay and I kept swapping them, and they were a mess.

One Sunday I decided to sort them. First into animals and birds. Then the animals into wild and pet. Then the wild ones into cats, dogs, bears. I made little boxes with labels.

Chinmay laughed. "Why is the tiger in two boxes?"

"It's not. It's in 'cats', and 'cats' is inside 'wild'."

Nature walk note, monsoon term.

On today's walk, Vinita, ten, collected leaves, stones and insects in her box. At the shelter, she sorted them without being asked: living and non-living, then living into plants and animals, then animals into insects and snails.

When a friend put a beetle with the stones, Vinita said, "It's alive, so it goes in the animal group, then in insects."

I'll set up a sorting table in class next week. — Ujjwal

Eid holidays, Thursday

Sudha and I sorted Nana's bookshelf today. It was a total mess.

First we made two piles: stories and not-stories. Then the stories into Urdu and English. Then the not-stories into science, history and cooking.

Sudha said the cooking books should go with science, because cooking is chemistry. We argued for ten minutes. We gave cooking its own little shelf inside "not-stories".

Nana came in and couldn't find his newspaper. But he found his old poetry book, which he hadn't seen for years.

Wasim

The art room at school smelled of paint and wet paper. Shreya Ma'am held up a print of a painting: fishermen's boats on a blue river at dawn.

"What do you notice?"

Jomon, ten, stared. "The water looks like it's moving."

"How?"

"The colours are small lines. Blue, then white, then pink."

Shreya Ma'am smiled. "Try it."

Jomon mixed blue and white and made tiny strokes. It didn't look like the print. He tried again with more water.

After the bell rang, he stayed back. "Ma'am, can I take the print home to look at?"

I'm Binita from the flat below. This winter, I often saw Hemant, eleven, on the terrace at dawn when the fog was thick.

He would stand very still, looking at the rooftops disappearing into white. Some mornings he had a pencil and paper and drew only lines, very faint.

Once I heard shehnai music from his phone. He closed his eyes.

I asked him what he was drawing. He said, "The fog. It's hard." I don't know what he felt, but he stayed out in the cold longer than anyone.
